Introduction Global environmental policy is continuing to place pressure on the transportation sector to decarbonize.91 This is an important step to meeting national and international carbon emissions goals set out for 2030, 2050, and beyond. One segment of the transportation sector that is lagging in terms of adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is the medium- and heavy-duty (MDHD) segment92. Relatively few efforts have been made to understand and model the MDHD fleet purchase process, including how purchasers view costs and benefits of EVs. Studies that have sought to model the adoption of MDHD EVs have used tools such as surveys, cost-benefit analysis, and Bass-type adoption curves93,94. Due to the high costs of survey-based research methods, the sparsity of data, and the inability of methods to rank the categories of consideration for MDHD purchasers, there is a distinct lack of knowledge about purchaser and consumer preference related to MDHD EVs. To fill this gap, we use the tools of text analytics to investigate the perceptions, views, opinions, and sentiments expressed by, or about, prospective MDHD fleet purchasers (e.g., fleet managers) that appear in the professional, academic, and trade literature. When considering only coherence results, the researcher must observe and speculate on the set of extracted word clusters and must infer the meaning behind the combination of words in a cluster96. For our purposes of implementing the results of this experiment in technology adoption models, a more specific quantification of the importance of the selected topics and terms will provide the researcher with an improved understanding of the purchasers’ considerations, and will provide quantitative outputs that can be incorporated into follow-up analyses. Our work deviates from the traditional systematic literature review in that it sources texts from peer reviewed and academic journals, as well as trade-journals. Upon introducing a new metric called the “Score of Topic and Related Terms” (START), we demonstrate use of the metric to enumerate the differences in focus between the texts associated with academia and with trade- journals. Each body of texts, or corpus, is used to fit two complimentary topic models. Results from this process are used to determine the importance of pre-determined categories within each corpus.
